title: Borrowing and Credit
blurb: Loan payments, credit scores, how lenders decide, and buying vs leasing vs mortgages

terms.def: Paying a loan off with equal payments, where each payment covers that month's interest first and the rest reduces the balance.
terms.example: Early mortgage payments are mostly interest; by the end they are mostly principal.

terms.def: The amount you borrowed, or still owe, not counting interest.
terms.example: Borrow $10,000 and the principal is $10,000. After two years of payments the principal left might be $6,100.

terms.def: The fixed amount paid each month on an amortizing loan, set so the balance reaches zero at the end.
terms.example: $20,000 over 5 years at 6% APR is about $387 a month.
terms.formula: PMT = P × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)^−N), where i = APR ÷ 12 and N = months

terms.def: Everything paid over the life of a loan minus the amount borrowed.
terms.example: $387 × 60 months = $23,220 paid on a $20,000 loan, so $3,220 of interest.

terms.def: A fee charged to set up a loan, usually a percent of the amount. It raises the true cost even when the rate looks low.
terms.example: A 3% fee on a $10,000 loan costs $300 on day one.

terms.def: Paying more than the required amount. All of the extra reduces the principal, so you save interest and finish sooner.
terms.example: Adding $50 a month to a $387 car payment cuts months off the loan and saves hundreds in interest.

cards.title: Every payment has two parts
cards.body: Each month the lender first charges interest on what you still owe. Whatever is left of your payment reduces the principal. Early on the balance is big, so most of the payment is interest. Later the balance is small, so most of it goes to principal.

cards.title: One month of a car loan
cards.body: You owe $20,000 at 6% APR. The monthly rate is 6% ÷ 12 = 0.5%, so this month's interest is $20,000 × 0.005 = $100. If your payment is $387, then $287 pays down principal and next month you owe $19,713.

cards.title: The payment formula
cards.body: PMT = P × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)^−N), where P is the amount borrowed, i the monthly rate (APR ÷ 12) and N the number of months. Total interest = PMT × N − P. To compare offers, add any fees to the total cost.

cards.title: Common mistake
cards.body: Picking the loan with the lowest monthly payment. Stretching a loan from 4 to 7 years lowers the payment but can add thousands in total interest. Compare total cost, fees included.

checks.prompt: You owe $12,000 at 12% APR. How much interest is charged this month?
A loan of $12,000 is repaid with 48 payments of $300. What is the total interest?
Where does an extra $100 payment go?
checks.explanation: Extra payments reduce the principal, so all future interest is charged on a smaller balance.

terms.def: A number from about 300 to 850 that estimates how likely you are to repay. Higher scores get cheaper loans.
terms.example: A 780 score might get a 6% car loan while a 600 score is offered 14%.

terms.def: How much of your credit card limits you are using. Under 30% helps your score and under 10% is best.
terms.example: A $600 balance on a $2,000 limit is 30% utilization.

terms.def: Your record of paying on time. It is the biggest part of a credit score, and a payment 30 or more days late can drop it sharply.
terms.example: Paying every bill on time for years builds the strongest score.

terms.def: How long your accounts have been open. Older accounts help, which is why closing your oldest card can hurt.
terms.example: Keeping a no-fee first card open adds years to your history.

terms.def: A lender checking your credit when you apply. Each one can dip your score a few points for a while.
terms.example: Applying for five cards in one month adds five hard inquiries.

terms.def: The smallest amount a card lets you pay. Paying only the minimum keeps you in debt for years and costs a lot of interest.
terms.example: $3,000 at 22% APR paying about 2% a month can take over 15 years to clear.

terms.def: The time between the statement date and the due date. Pay the full statement balance by then and a credit card charges no interest at all.
terms.example: Spend $600, pay the $600 statement balance by the due date: $0 interest.

cards.title: What goes into a score
cards.body: Roughly: payment history (35%), how much of your limits you use (30%), how long you have had credit (15%), the mix of credit types (10%) and new applications (10%). On-time payments and low utilization do most of the work. Income is not part of it at all.

cards.title: Utilization in action
cards.body: You have two cards: a $1,000 limit with $400 on it, and a $3,000 limit with $200 on it. Total balance $600 ÷ total limit $4,000 = 15% utilization. Paying the $400 card down before the statement date drops it to 5%.

cards.title: Quick numbers
cards.body: Utilization = balances ÷ limits. Aim for under 30%, ideally under 10%. A late payment stays on your report for 7 years, though its effect fades. Lenders often treat 740 and above as excellent.

cards.title: Common mistake
cards.body: Closing old cards to tidy up. It cuts your total limit, which raises utilization, and can shorten your history. Also, carrying a balance does not build credit: paying in full in time does the same job for free.

checks.prompt: Which factor matters most for a credit score?
checks.explanation: Paying on time is the biggest factor, about 35% of the score. Income isn't part of the score.

checks.prompt: You owe $900 across cards with $3,000 of total limits. What is your utilization?
Does carrying a balance from month to month help your credit score?
choices: No, paying in full works just as well and costs nothing
checks.explanation: Your score sees on-time payments and utilization. Interest on a carried balance is just a cost.

terms.def: Monthly debt payments, including the new loan, divided by monthly gross income. Lenders get cautious above about 36% and rarely go past 43 to 50%.
terms.example: $1,500 of payments on $5,000 a month of income is a 30% DTI.
terms.formula: DTI = monthly debt payments ÷ gross monthly income

terms.def: Something the lender can take if you don't repay, like a car or a house. Secured loans are safer for the lender, so they cost less.
terms.example: A car loan is secured by the car; a credit card is unsecured.

terms.def: The chance a borrower stops paying. Lower credit scores and higher DTI raise it.
terms.example: If 4 in 100 similar borrowers default, the probability of default is 4%.

terms.def: The share of a loan the lender loses when a borrower defaults, after selling any collateral.
terms.example: Lend $10,000 and recover $6,500 by selling the car: the loss given default is 35%.

terms.def: Charging riskier borrowers a higher rate so the extra interest covers their higher expected losses. The best borrowers get the prime rate.
terms.example: Prime borrowers get 7%; a borrower with a thin credit file might be offered 13%.

terms.def: Promising to repay someone else's loan if they don't. The debt counts against you and missed payments hurt your credit too.
terms.example: You co-sign a friend's $8,000 car loan; when they stop paying, the lender comes to you.

cards.title: Two questions every lender asks
cards.body: Can you afford it, and will you pay? Affordability is measured by debt-to-income. Track record shows up in the credit score. Collateral decides how much the lender loses if things go wrong.

cards.title: Underwriting one applicant
cards.body: Maya earns $6,000 a month and already pays $900 on a car and cards. The new loan would cost $600 a month. DTI = ($900 + $600) ÷ $6,000 = 25%. With a 720 score and the car as collateral, she is a low-risk borrower who can get the prime rate.

cards.title: Expected profit on a loan
cards.body: Expected profit ≈ (1 − chance of default) × interest margin earned − chance of default × loss given default. If 5% default and each default loses 75% of the loan, the expected loss is 0.05 × 75% = 3.75% of the loan, so the rate must earn more than that above the lender's own cost of money.

cards.title: Common mistake
cards.body: Thinking a high rate always means more profit. Charge strong borrowers too much and they take a loan elsewhere; charge risky borrowers too little and defaults eat the profit. Good pricing matches the rate to the risk, and some applications should simply be declined.

checks.prompt: Income $4,000 a month, existing debt payments $600, new loan payment $400. What is the DTI?
Why is a secured loan usually cheaper than an unsecured one?
choices: The lender can recover money from the collateral
checks.explanation: If the borrower defaults, selling the collateral cuts the lender's loss, so it can charge less.

checks.prompt: A lender expects 4% of borrowers to default, losing 50% of each loan. What is the expected loss as a share of the loan?

terms.def: Paying to use a car or other item for a few years without owning it. Payments are lower, but you hand it back with nothing to show and may owe mileage or wear fees.
terms.example: A $350 a month, 3-year lease costs $12,600 and you own nothing at the end.

terms.def: The loss in value of something as it ages. New cars often lose 15 to 20% of their value in the first year.
terms.example: A $30,000 car worth $24,000 after a year has depreciated $6,000.

terms.def: Everything something costs over the time you have it: price or payments, interest, fees, insurance and upkeep, minus what you can sell it for.
terms.example: Car: $25,000 price + $2,800 interest + $6,000 insurance − $12,000 resale = $21,800.

terms.def: A long loan, often 15 or 30 years, to buy a home, secured by the home itself.
terms.example: $300,000 over 30 years at 6% is about $1,799 a month.

terms.def: The part of a home or car price you pay upfront in cash. A bigger down payment means a smaller loan and less interest.
terms.example: 20% down on a $400,000 home is $80,000, leaving a $320,000 mortgage.

terms.def: The value of the best option you give up when you choose something. Money tied up in one place can't earn a return somewhere else.
terms.example: Putting $80,000 into a down payment gives up what it could have earned invested, perhaps $5,000 a year.

terms.def: A rise in an asset's value over time. Homes have historically appreciated a few percent a year on average, but not every year or everywhere.
terms.example: A $400,000 home appreciating 3% a year is worth about $464,000 after 5 years.

terms.def: Home price divided by a year of rent for a similar home. High ratios (above about 20) tend to favour renting; low ones favour buying.
Money a renter pays upfront that the landlord holds against damage or unpaid rent, returned at the end if the home is left in good shape.
terms.example: One month's rent of $1,400 held as a security deposit.

cards.title: Owning vs using
cards.body: Buying, with cash or a loan, means you own the item and keep its resale value. Leasing or renting means paying for use only: often cheaper month to month, but you build no ownership. The fair comparison is the total cost over the same period.

cards.title: Rent or buy, five years
cards.body: Renting: $2,000 a month rising 3% a year is about $127,000 over 5 years. Buying a $400,000 home: interest, property tax, insurance and upkeep might total $140,000, but the home may be worth more when you sell, and your $80,000 down payment could have earned a return if invested. Short stays usually favour renting because buying and selling costs are high.

cards.title: Tools
cards.body: Total cost of ownership = all payments + interest + fees + running costs − resale value. Opportunity cost of a down payment ≈ down payment × the return you could have earned. A mortgage payment uses the same loan formula: PMT = P × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)^−N).

cards.title: Common mistake
cards.body: Saying renting is throwing money away. Owners also pay money they never get back: interest, taxes, insurance and repairs. Which is cheaper depends on prices, rates and how long you stay.

checks.prompt: Why does a bigger down payment lower the total cost of a mortgage?
choices: You borrow less, so you pay less interest
Banks give a discount for cash
checks.explanation: Less borrowed means less interest every month for the whole loan.

checks.prompt: You will live in a city for only two years. What usually makes buying a poor choice?
choices: Homes never go up in value
Buying and selling costs are high compared with two years of rent
checks.explanation: Closing costs, agent fees and moving costs can wipe out any gain over a short stay.

checks.prompt: A car lease costs $300 a month for 36 months plus $2,000 upfront. What is the total paid?
checks.explanation: $300 × 36 = $10,800, plus $2,000 = $12,800, and you don't own the car at the end.
